title: The "Made with AI" label: what each platform actually requires in 2026.
deck: TikTok, YouTube, and Meta now enforce three different disclosure regimes for AI content — and the penalties for guessing wrong landed this year. Here is the map.
imageAlt: Close-up of a humanoid robot face representing artificial intelligence
body: If you publish the same video to TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram in 2026, you may be required to label it as AI-generated on one platform, encouraged to on another, and not asked at all on the third. Disclosure has become platform-specific — and the cost of getting it wrong stopped being theoretical this year.

- **TikTok — strictest.** Any AI-generated or significantly altered realistic depiction of people, places, or events needs a visible label: voice clones, AI avatars that put words in someone's mouth, simulated events. Automated detection backs the policy, and reporting this year describes a costly stick — videos caught unlabeled can forfeit Creator Fund earnings for two weeks, even after the label is added retroactively.
- **YouTube — self-declared.** The policy (introduced March 2024, enforced since early 2025) targets "realistic altered or synthetic content" that could mislead viewers. Creators flag it at upload; clearly stylized or obviously creative AI work is exempt, and AI-assisted content remains monetizable within originality rules.
- **Meta — unified this February.** Instagram and Facebook now surface an in-post "Made with AI" tag above the content, like a paid-partnership label, applied via advanced settings — and Meta auto-applies it when provenance metadata is detected, whether you asked or not.

The meaningful carve-out on all three: AI used for text, planning, or post-production that does not alter how people or scenes appear is exempt. Using an assistant to draft your script does not trigger a label. Cloning a voice does.

1. **Inventory your pipeline** — flag which steps touch the pixels and the audio, not just the words. That is the line every platform draws.
2. **Label realistic synthetic media everywhere, unprompted** — retroactive fixes no longer undo penalties on TikTok.
3. **Treat provenance metadata as a decision, not an accident** — mainstream AI tools embed it, and it can trigger automatic labeling downstream.

The disclosure era has a quieter implication, too: audiences are learning to read the labels. Creators who are matter-of-fact about their process — what was AI-assisted, what was handmade — are finding the tag costs them less than the appearance of hiding it would.
